hints: A Type I error is rejecting $\text{H}_0$ when it is true, so use $p=0.2$: $X\sim\text{B}(40,0.2)$. Test whether $X\leqslant2$ can be the rejection region by writing $\text{P}(0)+\text{P}(1)+\text{P}(2)$, each term ${}^{40}\text{C}_r\,0.2^r\,0.8^{40-r}$.
Evaluate the three terms and add them. Compare the total with the significance level of $2.5\%$: is it within it?
Check the next value as well: add $\text{P}(X=3)={}^{40}\text{C}_3\times0.2^3\times0.8^{37}$ to your total and compare that with $2.5\%$. Does the region grow to include $3$?
The probability of a Type I error is the probability of the rejection region you settled on, calculated with $p=0.2$. It is that probability, not the significance level, that you quote.
walkthrough:
**Set up the test**

Let $p$ be the proportion of households in Laxmi's town that contain more than $4$ people. The national figure is $20\%$, and she thinks her town's figure is lower:

$$\text{H}_0:\ p=0.2\qquad\text{H}_1:\ p<0.2$$

Let $X$ be the number out of $40$ households that have more than $4$ people. If $\text{H}_0$ is true, each household independently has probability $0.2$, so

$$X\sim\text{B}(40,\,0.2)$$

The alternative says $p$ is lower, so we reject $\text{H}_0$ when $X$ is small. The test is at the $2.5\%$ level, so we look for the biggest cut-off $c$ for which $\text{P}(X\leqslant c)\leqslant0.025$.

**What a Type I error is**

A Type I error means rejecting $\text{H}_0$ when $\text{H}_0$ is actually true. If $\text{H}_0$ is true then $p=0.2$, so the probability of a Type I error is the probability that $X$ falls in the rejection region when $X\sim\text{B}(40,0.2)$.

So the first job is to find the rejection region.

**Try X ≤ 2: write the probabilities (this earns the M1)**

The binomial formula is $\text{P}(X=r)={}^{n}\text{C}_r\,p^r\,q^{n-r}$ with $n=40$, $p=0.2$ and $q=1-p=0.8$.

$$\text{P}(X\leqslant2)=\text{P}(0)+\text{P}(1)+\text{P}(2)$$

$$\text{P}(0)={}^{40}\text{C}_0\times0.2^0\times0.8^{40}=0.8^{40}$$

$$\text{P}(1)={}^{40}\text{C}_1\times0.2\times0.8^{39}=40\times0.8^{39}\times0.2$$

$$\text{P}(2)={}^{40}\text{C}_2\times0.2^2\times0.8^{38}$$

The scheme wants to see these expressions written down.

**Compare with 0.025 (this earns the A1)**

$$\text{P}(X\leqslant2)=0.00794\ (<0.025)$$

So $X\leqslant2$ is small enough to be inside a $2.5\%$ rejection region. But is it the **biggest** such region? We must check the next value, $3$.

**Try X ≤ 3 (this earns the B1FT)**

$$\text{P}(X=3)={}^{40}\text{C}_3\times0.2^3\times0.8^{37}$$

${}^{40}\text{C}_3=\dfrac{40\times39\times38}{3\times2\times1}=\dfrac{59\,280}{6}=9880$. Also $0.2^3=0.008$ and $0.8^{37}=0.00025961$. So $9880\times0.008=79.04$ and $79.04\times0.00025961=0.0205199$.

$$\text{P}(X\leqslant3)=0.0079421+0.0205199=0.0284620\approx0.0285>0.025$$

This is bigger than $0.025$, so $3$ is **not** allowed in the rejection region. This second comparison is needed to show why the region stops at $2$.

**The probability of a Type I error (this earns the final B1)**

The rejection region is $X\leqslant2$. The probability that $X$ lands there when $\text{H}_0$ is true is the probability of a Type I error:

$$\text{P}(\text{Type I error})=\text{P}(X\leqslant2)=0.00794$$

A common slip is to answer $0.025$. The $2.5\%$ is only the limit we were allowed (the significance level). Because the binomial is discrete, the actual probability is smaller, $0.00794$.

walkthrough:
**Use the working from part (a)**

The rejection region is the set of results that make us reject $\text{H}_0$. For this lower-tail test it has the form $X\leqslant c$, where $c$ is the largest value with $\text{P}(X\leqslant c)\leqslant0.025$.

From part (a):

$$\text{P}(X\leqslant2)=0.00794\leqslant0.025\ \checkmark$$

$$\text{P}(X\leqslant3)=0.0285>0.025\ \times$$

So $c=2$.

**Final answer**

The rejection region is $X\leqslant2$ (that is, $X=0,1$ or $2$).

hints: A Type II error means $\text{H}_0$ is not rejected although it is false. Compare Laxmi's result of $2$ households with your rejection region from part (b): what does the test do with that result?
walkthrough:
**What a Type II error is**

A Type II error happens when we do **not** reject $\text{H}_0$, but $\text{H}_0$ is actually false. So to make a Type II error you must first fail to reject $\text{H}_0$.

The two errors are easy to mix up: Type I = rejecting a true $\text{H}_0$; Type II = keeping a false $\text{H}_0$.

**Look at Laxmi's result**

Laxmi finds exactly $2$ households with more than $4$ people, so $X=2$.

From part (b) the rejection region is $X\leqslant2$. The value $2$ is inside it.

**Conclude**

Because $X=2$ is in the rejection region, the test **rejects** $\text{H}_0$. Since $\text{H}_0$ is not kept, a Type II error cannot happen. (If anything went wrong it could only be a Type I error.)

**Final answer**

$\text{H}_0$ will be rejected, because the result $X=2$ lies in the rejection region. A Type II error needs $\text{H}_0$ to be accepted, so it is impossible.
